content: Some healthcare providers advocate for the routine use of episiotomy, a surgical incision made in the vaginal and perineal area during childbirth, as a means to prevent severe tears. However, performing an episiotomy inherently causes perineal trauma and necessitates suturing. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of a selective episiotomy policy (performed only when deemed necessary) compared to a routine episiotomy policy (performed as part of standard care) on maternal and neonatal outcomes during vaginal births. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared selective versus routine episiotomy, regardless of parity, clinical setting, or type of episiotomy performed. Trials involving both unassisted and assisted vaginal births were included, but quasi-RCTs, cross-over trials, and studies published only in abstract form were excluded. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two authors, with a third author resolving disagreements. Standardized methods for data analysis were employed, and results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The updated review incorporated 12 studies involving 6,177 women. Eleven studies focused on women undergoing labor with the intention of vaginal birth, while one study included women anticipating assisted vaginal delivery. Two large trials (each with over 1,000 participants) were conducted in Argentina and the UK, while smaller trials were conducted in Canada, Germany, Spain, Ireland, Malaysia, Pakistan, Colombia, and Saudi Arabia. Eight trials included only primiparous women, while four included both primiparous and multiparous women. In terms of methodological quality, nine trials adequately concealed allocation, three adequately reported random sequence generation, one trial adequately blinded outcome assessors, and one trial reported blinding of participants and personnel. For women anticipating unassisted vaginal births, a selective episiotomy policy was associated with a 30% reduction in the risk of severe perineal or vaginal trauma (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.94; 5,375 women; eight RCTs; low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding differences in blood loss at delivery was inconclusive, with an average of 27 mL less blood loss in the selective episiotomy group (95% CI ranging from 75 mL less to 20 mL more; two trials, 336 women; very low-certainty evidence). Both selective and routine episiotomy policies had little to no effect on the likelihood of infants having an Apgar score below seven at five minutes (four trials, no events; 3,908 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, there may be little to no difference in the risk of perineal infection between the two policies (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.82; three trials, 1,467 participants; low-certainty evidence). Regarding pain, the evidence was insufficient to determine whether selective episiotomy reduced the number of women experiencing moderate or severe perineal pain at three days postpartum (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.05; one trial, 165 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Long-term outcomes, such as dyspareunia (painful intercourse) at six months or more, showed little to no difference between the two policies (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.53; three trials, 1,107 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, there may be little to no difference in long-term urinary incontinence (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.44; three trials, 1,107 participants; low-certainty evidence). One trial reported on genital prolapse at three years postpartum, finding no clear difference between the two groups (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.41; 365 women; one trial; low-certainty evidence). Other long-term outcomes, such as urinary fistula, rectal fistula, and fecal incontinence, were not reported. Subgroup analyses based on parity (primiparous versus multiparous women) and surgical method (midline versus mediolateral episiotomy) did not reveal any modifying effects. Pain was not well-assessed across studies, and women's preferences were not reported. In a trial involving women undergoing operative vaginal delivery (175 participants), no clear difference in severe perineal trauma was observed between selective and routine episiotomy policies. However, the analysis was underpowered to detect significant differences. In conclusion, for women not undergoing instrumental delivery, selective episiotomy policies result in fewer cases of severe perineal or vaginal trauma. Other shortand long-term outcomes do not provide clear evidence of harm to the mother or baby with selective episiotomy. The belief that routine episiotomy reduces perineal or vaginal trauma is not supported by current evidence. Further research is needed to clarify the role of routine episiotomy in women undergoing instrumental delivery, with an emphasis on standardized outcome assessment methods.
